newsitem.title: GERMANY: German opposition SPD rejects pension reform talks.
newsitem.headline: German opposition SPD rejects pension reform talks.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said on Monday they were not willing to enter talks with the government aimed at cross-party consensus for a planned reform of the country's pension system.

SPD chief Oskar Lafontaine said after a meeting of party executives in Bonn that the SPD was ready to debate the reform within normal parliamentary business but that they saw no point in special talks on the issue.

Bonn is seeking to reduce pension levels in a bid to cope with the country's ageing population and as part of structural reforms it says are necessary ahead of Europe's planned monetary union and with increasingly globalised economies.
Current proposals envisage dropping pension levels to 64 percent of average net wages from around 70 percent.
But Lafontaine said the SPD would not allow pension levels to fall close to the level at which many pensioners would then need additional welfare payments.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) do not need the agreement of the SPD to pass the reform into law. Without opposition agreement, however, they risk seeing any pension cuts become a potentially damaging 1998 election issue.
